blog_summary: The blog post discusses a paper that explores the concept of 'virtual democracy' as a framework for making automated decisions in noisy and uncertain environments, using a food bank donation distribution system as a case study. The key idea is to learn the voting preferences of stakeholders (donors, recipients, volunteers, etc.) through pairwise comparisons and then use a voting rule to combine these learned preferences into a final decision. The paper focuses on the robustness of voting rules to noise, particularly the Borda count rule, which is shown to be highly robust compared to other voting rules like pairwise-majority consistent (PMC) rules. The authors leverage the Mallows model to validate their approach and demonstrate that the Borda count's robustness stems from its linear dependence on the separation of scores, making it unlikely to produce incorrect decisions even with noisy inputs. The paper also highlights the explainability of the Borda count, as decisions can be easily justified by average positions and feature importance.
paper_authors: Kahng, A. and Frazier, P. I. and Gupta, S. and Udell, M.
paper_abstract: Virtual democracy is an approach to automating decisions, by learning models of the preferences of individual people, and, at runtime, aggregating the predicted preferences of those people on the dilemma at hand. One of the key questions is which aggregation method — or voting rule — to use; we offer a novel statistical viewpoint that provides guidance. Specifically, we seek voting rules that are robust to prediction errors, in that their output on people’s true preferences is likely to coincide with their output on noisy estimates thereof. We prove that the classic Borda count rule is robust in this sense, whereas any voting rule belonging to the wide family of pairwisemajority consistent rules is not. Our empirical results further support, and more precisely measure, the robustness of Borda count.
